newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry welcomes central bank policy.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry welcomes central bank policy.

text.p: India's new six-month monetary policy announced by the central bank on Saturday will help the country tide over a recent slowdown in industrial growth and boost exports, top industry associations said.
"This may arrest the slowdown of the industrial and export growth," said a statement by the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India (Assocham).

The Reserve Bank of India signalled a cut in interest rates by announcing reduced banks' cash reserve ratios and deposit interest rates. RBI cut the cash reserve ratio (CRR) on banks to 10 percent from 12 percent to be implemented in four stages.

"The reduction in CRR... would provide the industry the much needed credit thereby mitigating the hardship which the industry was facing and help arrest the slowdown in industrial and exports growth," Shekhar Datta, president of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) said in a statement.
"The market was looking forward to the central bank to increase liquidity into the system and RBI has matched the sentiments while doing a fine balancing act," Datta said.
Assocham said the impact of the CRR cut was uncertain.

"A mere supply of money may not lower the interest rate unless and until other steps like efficient management of government's revenue and expenditure are taken and the operational efficency of the banking system is improved," Assocham said.
The central bank announced a cut in the interest cap on term deposits of 30 days to one year maturity to 10 percent from 11 percent.
CII's Datta said he was disappointed by this move as he had expected a total freeing of interest rates.
RBI said it would raise banks' export credit target to 12 percent from 10 percent.
"The recognition of the RBI to promote exports and thereby increase the share of credit to exporters...is a step in the right direction," Datta said.
Assocham cheered RBI's decision to allow banks to trade in shares and debentures in the secondary markets but added that the impact may be minimal.

"This may not have a very positive impact on the existing sluggish capital market. Assocham is of the view that an additional limit of 5 percent should have been introduced," the industry association said.
Banks are allowed to purchase shares in primary and secondary markets only within the existing limit of 5 percent of incremental deposits.
